value.body: A regulatory affairs associate prepares, compiles and tracks the documents a pharma company needs to get its medicines approved and keep them compliant after launch. Employers include pharma and generic-drug manufacturers, contract research organisations and regulatory service firms. Most days are desk work: drafting dossier sections, checking labels, answering regulator queries and tracking submission deadlines.

items.label: Typical entry
items.note: An M.Pharm in Regulatory Affairs is a common add-on

items.label: Indian regulator
items.value: CDSCO, under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940

items.label: Common formats and tools
items.value: CTD / eCTD dossiers, the SUGAM portal, Word and Excel

items.label: Pharmaceutical exports
items.note: Each export market needs its own regulatory filings

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Freshers usually join regulatory teams as trainee or junior associates after a B.Pharm, M.Pharm or Pharm.D. A short regulatory affairs certificate can help but is not required, and some people start in quality assurance or documentation and move across later.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Writing and formatting dossier sections in CTD format
Reading regulatory guidelines from CDSCO, US FDA, EMA and WHO
Reviewing labels, leaflets and packaging text for compliance
Tracking submissions, regulator queries and licence renewals
Careful document control and version tracking

value.title: At a glance
items: A common progression is associate, senior associate, then regulatory affairs manager.
Export-focused companies need knowledge of rules in overseas markets such as the US, EU and emerging markets.
The work is desk-based and deadline-driven, with little patient or field contact.
